## The symptom

Reported as EI-21860314946358337 (2nd independent report, promoted from probation): a same-turn fan-out of `work_items:checkpoint`, `loop:checkpoint`, and `coord:send` — three separate `ptool` CLI invocations fired concurrently from the same shell/turn — left all three client processes sitting in `epoll_wait` (confirmed via process inspection) for **more than two minutes**, with no output from any of them. The reporting agent killed the three stuck processes, verified via content hash that none of the writes had landed (no double-write risk), then retried each **sequentially** with output captured to a file. Every retry completed in **4-10 seconds**.

That contrast — instant failure-free success in sequence, multi-minute silent hang under concurrency, for the *exact same three calls* — is the tell.

## Root cause: ptool is a one-shot process; concurrency multiplies HANDSHAKE contention, not call contention

`ptool.mjs` is documented as "An interactive CLI for invoking any `defineTool` endpoint from the terminal" (top-of-file comment) — it is explicitly **not** a persistent client. Every single `ptool <verb>` invocation from the shell is a brand-new Node process whose `main()` does, in order (apps/operator/scripts/ptool.mjs:1848-1905):

1. `new StreamableHTTPClientTransport(url, ...)`
2. `new Client(...)`
3. `await client.connect(transport, { timeout: PTOOL_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS })` — a full MCP session `initialize` handshake
4. `listToolsWithLocalRetry(...)` / `client.listTools(...)` — a `tools/list` discovery call
5. **only then** the actual `tools/call`

Steps 3 and 4 are write-free MCP **control-plane** requests. The operator's MCP proxy (`apps/operator/lib/mcp-proxy/proxy.ts`) admits these through a **class-specific, bounded pool** (`maxHandshakeInFlight` / `RESERVED_CONTROL_PLANE_TOOLS`), separate from the pool used for ordinary `tools/call` forwards, with a bounded FIFO (`maxHandshakeQueueWaitMs`) once that pool is full. Under real fleet load — many concurrent agents, each spawning their own `ptool`/`mcp-call.mjs` processes for shell-level tool calls — this handshake pool is frequently near its ceiling.

A **single** `ptool` call pays this handshake cost once, then makes its one `tools/call` and exits — cheap, and usually fast (4-10s matches the reported sequential timing). But **N concurrently-launched `ptool` processes each independently pay the full connect+list handshake at the same moment**, multiplying the instantaneous handshake-admission pressure by N. If the handshake pool is already under pressure from the wider fleet, several of these N processes queue for a handshake slot, race retries (`PTOOL_CONNECT_MAX_ATTEMPTS` at `PTOOL_CONNECT_RETRY_DELAY_MS` ≈1s intervals) against `PTOOL_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS`, and can spend well over a minute just reaching the point where their actual `tools/call` is dispatched — before ever touching whatever specific tool-call lane (e.g. the shared single-flight `criticalContinuationAgent` socket that `work_items:checkpoint`/`loop:checkpoint` share) the report might otherwise implicate.

This explains why **`coord:send` hung too**, even though it has its own dedicated one-socket lane for the actual call (`EI-21669304707115602`): that dedicated lane only governs the *tools/call* phase. The handshake phase in front of it is shared, unbundled, and paid fresh by every `ptool` process regardless of which tool it will eventually call.

It also explains the clean sequential result: once the concurrent burst that caused momentary handshake contention is gone, each subsequent lone `ptool` invocation finds the handshake pool has headroom and completes in seconds — exactly as observed.

## What this is *not*

- **Not evidence of a deadlock or bug in the single-flight critical-continuation socket** (`work_items:checkpoint`/`loop:checkpoint`/`work_items:complete`/`improvements:capture`/`session:request-compaction`/`loop:end` share one socket with a bounded — 20s — dwell for most of them, and an intentionally *unbounded* dwell specifically for `work_items:checkpoint`, "the fallback record for this boundary"). A direct repro of two of these fired concurrently from an already-connected persistent MCP client (a live su session's own tool calls, which skip the handshake phase entirely because the session connection is already established) completed with no observable delay — consistent with the handshake phase, not the call-routing lane, being the actual bottleneck for the `ptool`-CLI case.
- **Not a lost-write risk.** The reporting agent verified content hashes were unchanged before killing the stuck processes — none of the three writes had reached the handler.

## Diagnosing a similar report

- Symptom: several **`ptool`-launched (or `scripts/mcp-call.mjs`-launched, same one-shot-process design)** CLI invocations, fired concurrently from the same shell/turn, all hang with zero output for well past their individual tools' normal runtime; a `ps`/process inspection shows them parked in `epoll_wait`; killing and retrying the SAME calls sequentially succeeds quickly.
- This is the class match. Check: were the calls launched as separate OS processes (ptool/mcp-call.mjs), or as parallel tool calls from an already-connected persistent client (a live MCP session)? Only the former pays the per-invocation handshake cost N times.

## Guidance

- **Prefer a persistent client's own parallel tool-call dispatch** (e.g. a Claude/Codex session's native tool-call batching within one turn) over fanning out several concurrent `ptool`/`mcp-call.mjs` CLI processes from a shell script — the persistent client pays the handshake once per session, not once per call.
- **When a shell script genuinely must fire several `ptool` calls together**, serialize them (as the reporting agent's successful workaround did) rather than backgrounding them concurrently with `&`; the aggregate wall-clock cost of N sequential ptool calls at 4-10s each is usually far cheaper than the tail risk of concurrent handshake contention running one of them past a multi-minute silent hang.
- No code fix is proposed here: ptool's one-shot-process design is intentional (it must resolve `@inquirer/prompts`/the MCP SDK from the operator's own `node_modules` and needs no server-side session state between invocations), and the handshake admission bulkhead it competes for is itself a deliberate, load-tested defense against a *different* failure class (see the proxy.ts EI-19305299022434394/EI-21504897841052086 history). This doc exists so the NEXT report of "concurrent ptool calls hang, sequential retries succeed" is recognized as this same class in minutes rather than re-diagnosed from scratch.
